extracted.intended_audience: People of the State of New York; citizens deciding on ratification of the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political essays arguing for adoption of the proposed federal Constitution by explaining dangers of disunion and the advantages of a confederate republic. The pieces marshal historical examples and practical consequences to persuade voters and legislators to support union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial disputes as a fertile source of hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations ... This cause would exist among us in full force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Unsettled Western territory and discordant claims between States would revive on dissolution of the Union. Examples: conflicting colonial/crown land claims; Connecticut vs Pennsylvania (Wyoming) and disputes involving Vermont. Practical consequence: without a federal adjudicator, apportionment and competing principles for division would lead to prolonged disagreement and likely resort to force. Anti-pattern: assuming past peaceful settlements imply future peaceful resolution absent a common authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a common umpire/judge invites interstate conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: In the wide field of Western territory, therefore, we perceive an ample theatre for hostile pretensions, without any umpire or common judge to interpose between the contending parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: A federal authority or tribunal is required to settle interstate controversies impartially; otherwise disputes over territory, commerce, or debt will escalate. Example: Articles of Confederation required submission to a federal court, but dissatisfaction (e.g., Connecticut's reluctance) shows fragility of such mechanisms when Union is weak. Design implication: provide durable, enforceable federal adjudicatory powers to prevent armed arbitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial competition between sovereign states will produce reprisals and war
rubrics_metrics.description: The competitions of commerce would be another fruitful source of contention ... Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue a system of commercial policy peculiar to itself. This would occasion distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, which would beget discontent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Divergent state tariffs, trade regulations, and privileges will produce perceptions of injury and actual economic harm leading to infractions, enforcement measures, reprisals, and eventually armed conflict. Example: New York's duties benefiting its metropolis could be seen as taxation for New York's exclusive benefit, antagonizing Connecticut and New Jersey. Design implication: national uniformity or arbitration in commercial policy reduces incentives for inter-state retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debt apportionment will engender ill-humor, animosity, and possible noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. The apportionment, in the first instance, and the progressive extinguishment afterward, would be alike productive of ill-humor and animosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: No apportionment rule is free from objection; differing stakes (creditor-heavy vs debtor-heavy states) create conflicting incentives, procrastination, refusal to pay, and public clamour. Causes of delinquency include differing resources, mismanagement, and reluctance to pay for past exigencies. Practical consequence: foreign pressures for satisfaction could compound internal tensions. Design implication: credible national mechanisms for debt assumption, apportionment, and enforcement are necessary to preserve peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws violating private contracts provoke interstate retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws in violation of private contracts, as they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them, may be considered as another probable source of hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: State legislation that impairs contracts of citizens from other states invites reproach and retaliatory measures. Example: Retaliation excited in Connecticut by actions of Rhode Island's legislature. Practical consequence: such legislative aggressions could escalate to military reprisals if no federal remedy exists. Design implication: constitutional protection of contracts and federal recourse reduces causes for inter-state retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incompatible foreign alliances will entangle parts of the country and threaten the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of incompatible alliances between the different States or confederacies and different foreign nations ... America, if not connected at all, or only by the feeble tie of a simple league, would, by the operation of such jarring alliances, be gradually entangled in all the pernicious labyrinths of European politics and wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Separate states forming distinct alliances with foreign powers will drag other parts into external conflicts and be subject to manipulation. Practical consequence: divide et impera—foreign powers hostile to the whole would exploit disunity. Design implication: unified foreign policy under federal authority prevents destructive entanglements and exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disunion breeds standing armies and erosion of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent war and constant apprehension ... will infallibly produce [standing armies] ... Standing armies ... increase the executive at the expense of the legislative authority ... our liberties would be a prey to the means of defending ourselves against the ambition and jealousy of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Internal interstate war or frequent external threats lead states to raise disciplined standing armies and fortifications, which strengthen executive power and tend toward despotism. Comparative example: continental European powers vs. Britain's insular situation; in America lack of fortifications and militia traditions would make conquests easier and standing armies more likely. Design implication: union reduces the need for large standing armies and helps protect civil liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlargement of the republican orbit (larger republic/confederate republic) represses faction and insurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: I mean the ENLARGEMENT of the ORBIT within which such systems are to revolve ... The utility of a Confederacy, as well to suppress faction and to guard the internal tranquillity of States, as to increase their external force and security, is in reality not a new idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Larger size or a confederate republic dilutes the influence of particular factions, makes majority tyranny less likely, and enables the association to resist external force without internal corruption. Quoted Montesquieu passages: confederate republics combine internal republican advantages with external monarchical force. Design implication: a union/comprehensive confederacy is a corrective to the factional instability of small republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve state governments as constituent parts while vesting necessary federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution ... makes [State governments] constituent parts of the national sovereignty, by allowing them a direct representation in the Senate, and leaves in their possession certain exclusive and very important portions of sovereign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: A confederate republic need not abolish separate state organizations; federal authority's extent, modifications, and objects are discretionary. Practical consequence: a well-designed union can retain local self-government while empowering a general government to handle common concerns (representation in Senate cited as structural safeguard). Design implication: constitutional structure should balance federal powers with retained state sovereign functions to secure both union and local autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal jealousies and motives to dismemberment create danger without union
rubrics_metrics.description: In a review of these transactions we may trace some of the causes which would be likely to embroil the States with each other, if it should be their unpropitious destiny to become disunited ... Small States ... saw with an unfriendly eye the perspective of our growing greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Political jealousy, fears of future power, and interests of influential individuals (e.g., land grant holders) motivate other states to favor dismemberment or independence of parts. Examples: opposition to New York's claims from New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut; New Jersey and Rhode Island support for Vermont. Practical consequence: internal rivalries and sectional jealousies would be exploited absent a unifying constitution. Design implication: institutional arrangements should reduce incentives for dismemberment and mitigate jealousies among constituent units.
